source_refs.note: Book p. 53-54: 4.4 Determinants, the opening lines before 4.4.1 (pattern for order n >= 3, |A| of a 3 x 3 matrix); callouts marked Teaching note / Key points / Common mistake are ours.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What is a determinant? Every square matrix has one special number attached to it, called its determinant. For a matrix \(A\) we write it as \(|A|\) or \(\det A\). A matrix is a table of numbers; its determinant is a single number worked out from that table.
Why do we need it? In this unit the determinant tells us whether a matrix has an inverse (4.5): if \(|A| \ne 0\) the inverse exists, if \(|A| = 0\) it does not. Later it is also used to solve systems of linear equations (Cramer's rule).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Recall the determinant of order 2, which you met in earlier classes:
\[\begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = ad - bc\]
Multiply along the leading diagonal, then subtract the product along the other diagonal. For example
\[\begin{vmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 3(4) - 5(2) = 2\]
Every determinant of order 3 will be reduced to determinants of order 2, so this rule must be automatic for you.

Now our aim is to compute the determinants of matrices of various orders.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Notice the two kinds of brackets. Square brackets \([\;\,]\) mean a matrix (a table). Straight vertical bars \(|\;\,|\) mean its determinant (one number). So \(A\) is a matrix but \(|A|\) is a number.
Only a square matrix (same number of rows and columns) has a determinant. A \(2 \times 3\) matrix has no determinant.

To compute \(|A|\) for order 3 we need two new ideas, the minor and the cofactor of an element (4.4.1). With them the determinant of order 3 is expanded in 4.4.2, its properties are listed in 4.4.3, and in 4.5 the cofactors are used again to find the inverse of a matrix.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. The determinant is a number attached to a square matrix only; it is written \(|A|\) or \(\det A\).
2. Order 2: \(\begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = ad - bc\).
3. Determinants of order 3 or more follow the same pattern and are worked out with minors and cofactors.
4. \(|A| \ne 0\) decides whether \(A\) has an inverse (4.5).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reading \(|A|\) as an absolute value. A determinant can be negative: \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 4 - 6 = -2\).
2. Writing \(ad + bc\) or \(bc - ad\) for order 2. It is always (leading diagonal) minus (other diagonal): \(ad - bc\).
3. Using square brackets for a determinant or bars for a matrix: the two mean different things.
4. Trying to find the determinant of a non-square matrix.
